analysis.one_liner: Requires the President to declare a national climate emergency and direct federal investment against it.
analysis.headline: Backed by 63 House Democrats and no Republicans, the bill was referred to seven committees, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required the President to formally declare climate change a national emergency under the National Emergencies Act. In responding, the President would have to steer large-scale federal investment into clean energy, building retrofits, public health, and resilience projects, with at least 40 percent of the money flowing to historically disadvantaged communities, and jobs paying family-sustaining wages with union rights. The bill itself contains no funding; it directs the executive branch to mobilize. It was referred to seven House committees, sent to two subcommittees, and never taken up again.
analysis.who_benefits: Communities hit hardest by pollution and extreme weather would be first in line for investment, since at least 40 percent of spending must go to historically disadvantaged communities. Workers would gain from jobs required to pay family-sustaining wages and protect the right to organize. Farmers, rural communities, small and minority-owned businesses, and clean-energy manufacturers would gain from directed federal spending. Everyone exposed to climate-driven floods, wildfires, and heat would benefit from the mitigation and resilience projects it mandates.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Frontline communities, workers, and clean-energy industries

how_it_helps.text: Requires the President to declare a national emergency with respect to climate change under the National Emergencies Act.

Directs federal investment in large-scale mitigation and resiliency projects, including upgrades to public energy, transportation, broadband, and water systems and retrofits of millions of homes, schools, and buildings to cut pollution and costs.

Requires that at least 40 percent of investments flow to historically disadvantaged communities, and directs the government to combat environmental injustice and prioritize hiring from marginalized communities.
Requires that jobs created under the response conform to labor standards providing family-sustaining wages and benefits, safe workplaces, and protection of workers' right to organize.
Directs investment in regenerative agriculture, local and regional food systems, and domestic clean-technology manufacturing, and requires annual presidential reports on actions taken.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers would fund the mobilization, though the bill sets no dollar figure and creates no appropriation. Fossil fuel companies would bear the largest cost: the bill's findings call for an economically just phase-out of oil, gas, and coal, and an emergency mobilization would accelerate investment away from those fuels. Utilities, refiners, and energy-intensive manufacturers could face higher costs from the required pollution cuts and building retrofits.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers and the fossil fuel industry

drawbacks.text: The bill uses the National Emergencies Act, which hands the President broad standby executive powers; it requires a declaration but does not itself define the specific programs, spending limits, or congressional checks that would govern how those powers are used beyond a required annual report.
The bill directs massive investment but contains no funding mechanism or cost estimate, so the price of the mobilization to taxpayers is unspecified and would depend on later spending bills.

Some of its requirements, such as the 40 percent community investment set-aside and union-standard hiring rules, could raise the cost and slow the pace of projects relative to awarding contracts purely on lowest cost.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill aimed a large federal mobilization at a problem — climate change — that its own findings describe as already costing roughly $100 billion a year in disasters, and it directed that spending toward communities and workers rather than letting it flow through private contractors on whatever terms the market sets. The trade-offs are real: emergency powers are a blunt instrument with limited oversight, the bill sets no budget, and its labor and equity requirements add cost and time. Whether that trade is worth it depends largely on how much weight one gives to the projected costs of inaction.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to seven House committees and two subcommittees on referral, and no committee ever held a hearing, marked it up, or voted on it; the Congress ended in January 2023 with the bill still stuck in committee.

narrative.text: Representative Earl Blumenauer introduced the bill on February 4, 2021, joined by original cosponsors including Representatives Ocasio-Cortez, Khanna, Jayapal, and Pressley.

The bill was referred to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and six other committees — Financial Services, Education and Labor, Energy and Commerce, Natural Resources, Agriculture, and Small Business.

Within a day it was sent to the Economic Development, Public Buildings, and Emergency Management Subcommittee and the Environment and Climate Change Subcommittee, and no further action of any kind followed.
All 62 cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican signed on.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2023, without the bill ever receiving a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers and other industries that would have faced an emergency-scale federal push away from oil, gas, and coal are better off because the bill never advanced, as are those wary of expanding presidential emergency powers. Communities on the front lines of pollution and climate disasters, who would have been first in line for its investment requirements, are no better off than before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers and skeptics of emergency powers

industries.note: The bill's findings call for an economically just phase-out of oil, gas, and coal, and an emergency mobilization would direct investment and policy away from fossil fuels. The bill never advanced, so these producers face no new requirements.

The bill directs investment in clean and affordable energy and prioritizes domestic clean-technology manufacturing, which would create demand for these industries while requiring good wages for the jobs created.

Retrofitting millions of homes, schools, offices, and industrial buildings would generate large-scale construction work, with the bill requiring family-sustaining wages and union protections on that work.
The bill requires jobs to meet union standards, protects the right to organize, and bars solutions that decrease union density, tilting emergency spending toward unionized work.
The bill directs investment in regenerative agriculture and local and regional food systems supporting farmers, agricultural workers, and soil health.
